summary: Unit tests for `iip/rules.py`, the pure rule engine. Because `detect`, `assess` and `compute_score` take plain dicts and a `History` dataclass and never touch the database, each rule can be tested in microseconds by building an event by hand and choosing exactly what the user's history says. Thresholds are probed on both sides of their boundary, so changing a weight or limit in `rules.py` makes a test fail immediately.

notes.text: Docstring stating the testing strategy: since `rules.py` is pure (no database, no I/O), these tests need no fixtures and no app.
`datetime` builds fixed timestamps and `timedelta` expresses gaps such as twenty minutes later.
pytest provides `parametrize` (run one test with many inputs) and `raises` (assert that an exception happens).
Imports the module itself (for constants such as `rules.WEIGHTS` and functions such as `rules.assess`) plus the four names used most often, so the tests read naturally.
A fixed reference time (1 January 2026, 12:00). Using a constant instead of the current time makes every test deterministic: the same inputs always produce the same time gaps.
Helper that builds a normalized event dict; keyword arguments override individual fields.

The baseline event deliberately triggers no rule: a successful login from Dubai (which `signals_for` treats as home), a known device, a clean documentation-range IP, zero failed attempts, and no transaction or resource. Its keys mirror the normalized event dict that `process_event` passes to `detect`.
Unpacks `base` and then `overrides` into a new dict. Later keys win, so `event(location="London, UK")` changes that one field and keeps every other default.
Helper that runs the detector and returns only the signal names. Extra keyword arguments become `History` fields such as `baseline_location` or `spray_accounts`.

Calls `detect` with a history whose home is Dubai and whose device is **not** trusted, so the `Trusted device` bonus never appears and assertions only see risk signals. The second return value (the enrichment context) is discarded with `_`.
Extracts the `signal` name from each `Finding` object.
Tests `compute_score`, which turns a list of signal names into a 0-100 score.
Additivity: New device (+15) plus Suspicious IP (+30) must equal exactly 45.
Lower clamp: Trusted device alone weighs -15, but a score can never go below 0.
Upper clamp: all positive weights added together come to 225, so the result must be capped at 100. Building the list from `rules.WEIGHTS` keeps the test valid if new signals are added later.

Runs the next test eight times, once per (score, level) pair. The pairs sit on both sides of every boundary (29/30, 59/60, 79/80) plus the extremes, exactly where an off-by-one mistake such as `>` instead of `>=` would show up.
Asserts that `classify` maps each score to the expected level using the `LEVELS` floors: CRITICAL from 80, HIGH from 60, MEDIUM from 30, otherwise LOW.
Sanity check: the untouched baseline event must raise no signals at all. If a rule fired here, every other test built on `event()` would be testing the wrong thing.
With `trusted_device=True` in the history and `device_new` false on the event, the only finding must be the negative-weight `Trusted device` signal, proving the risk-reducing rule works on its own.
Changes four fields at once: a new device, a city other than home, a malicious IP, and three failed attempts (exactly `FAILED_ATTEMPTS_THRESHOLD`).

Each identity rule must fire, and nothing else. Comparing sets means the order of findings doesn't matter. A `malicious` reputation counts as Suspicious IP because the rule only checks that the reputation is not `clean`.
The same user shows up in London 20 minutes after the reference time.

With Dubai as the trusted baseline 20 minutes earlier, the trip is about 5,470 km at roughly 16,400 km/h, far above the 900 km/h airliner limit, so `Impossible travel` must be raised. This proves the rule uses real distance and speed, not just a changed city label.
The docstring explains the regression this guards against: Abu Dhabi to Dubai is only about 120 km, within the error margin of IP geolocation, yet the old rule flagged it.
The move happens 20 minutes after the baseline. The distance is below `MIN_TRAVEL_KM` (500 km), so the rule refuses to call it impossible; the implied speed, about 370 km/h, is under the limit too.
Dubai to London again, but eight hours later, which is a realistic flight.
Calls `detect` directly to get the context as well. `History` is built positionally here: home Dubai, untrusted device, baseline location Dubai, baseline time `T0`.
The plausible trip must not be flagged.

The travel context is still recorded (it feeds the threat map), marked not impossible, with a speed (about 684 km/h) below `IMPOSSIBLE_SPEED_KMH`. Comparing against the constant keeps the test in step with the rulebook.
Atlantis has no coordinates, so no distance can be computed. The rule falls back to a time-window heuristic: any move within `UNKNOWN_CITY_WINDOW` (2 hours) is flagged, and 30 minutes qualifies.
Runs the next test twice: once with a suspicious IP reputation and once with a failed login.
An otherwise impossible Dubai-to-London trip in 20 minutes, combined with one of those two conditions.

Travel is only judged on successful, clean-IP events, so no `Impossible travel` may appear. The comment in `rules.detect` explains why: proxies and VPN exits make a flagged IP's location unreliable, so that risk is scored as Suspicious IP instead.
The trip is still computed, but the context records `assessed` as false, which is how the UI can show it as not judged rather than as plausible.

Four (amount, risky context, expected flag) cases: $12,000 is always suspicious (at or above `LARGE_TRANSACTION`, 10,000); $2,500 is suspicious only from a risky context; $500 never is, even from a new device. Underscores in `12_000` are just digit separators.
Builds a transaction where `risky` sets `device_new`, because a new device (or a flagged IP) is what makes the context risky.
The parenthesised membership test gives True or False, and `is expected` demands exactly that value, so the test fails both when the flag is missing and when it appears unexpectedly.
A tiny $5 transaction, so only the velocity rule can fire.

`recent_transactions` counts the user's earlier transactions in the 10-minute window, and the rule adds the current one. One earlier makes only two in total (no flag); two earlier make three, which reaches `RAPID_TRANSACTION_COUNT`.
A password-reset event, which the rule inspects together with the user's recent failed logins.
Two failed logins in the previous hour are not enough; three (`RESET_FAILURES`) are. Testing both sides pins the threshold exactly.
A failed login, because only failures can be part of a password spray.

`spray_accounts` counts **other** accounts that failed from the same IP in the last 30 minutes; the current account adds one. Three others make 4 accounts (no flag), four others make 5, which is `SPRAY_ACCOUNTS`.
Even with 10 other accounts failing from this IP, a **successful** login is never labelled a spray, as the inline comment says: the rule requires the event itself to be a failure.
Accessing `admin-console`, one of the `PRIVILEGED_RESOURCES`, must raise the privileged-access signal. The single assertion is just wrapped over two lines.
Runs detection on an event with a new device (+15) and a suspicious IP (+30). `detect` produces New device first, because that rule comes earlier in the code.
`assess` turns the raw findings into the decision dict that the API returns for every event.
15 + 30 = 45, which falls in the MEDIUM band (30-59).
Contributions must be ordered heaviest first, `[30, 15]`, the reverse of detection order. This proves `assess` sorts by weight, so the UI can show the biggest reason at the top.
The recommended action comes from the `ACTIONS` table for MEDIUM (Monitor and log).
The plain-English explanation names the signals that contributed.
`what_if` scores a hand-picked list of signals (the Risk Lab feature). The duplicated Suspicious IP is counted once because `what_if` removes duplicates with `dict.fromkeys`: 40 + 30 = 70, not 100.

An unknown signal name must raise `KeyError`; `pytest.raises` passes only if that exception happens inside the `with` block. The API rejects unknown names earlier with a 422, so this is the engine's own safety net.
Fetches the rulebook, the dict served by `GET /api/v1/risk/rules`.
Every defined signal must be listed, so the UI can never silently miss one.
Levels come out lowest to highest, the reverse of the internal `LEVELS` tuple, which is ordered highest first so that `classify` can pick the first floor the score reaches.
MITRE ATT&CK sub-techniques are written with a dot (`T1110.003`), but their web pages use a slash. The test proves the `mitre` property turns the ID into a working URL.
A signal with no ATT&CK mapping (the risk-reducing Trusted device) must return `None` rather than a broken link.
